title: SpondylolisthesisRelevant Anatomy
text:
Each lumbar vertebra has an anterior weight-bearing body and a posterior arch, formed by paired pedicles and laminae that enclose the spinal canal. The arch bears the spinous process, transverse processes, and superior and inferior articular processes, which form the facet joints. The vertebral bodies from L1 to L5 enlarge caudally, while L4–L5 take on transitional features that shape lower-lumbar loading.






NoteKey idea



The immature spine’s open growth plates and secondary ossification centers make it more susceptible to injury. This is one reason spondylolysis often begins in childhood or adolescence.





Source: OrthoEducation.

title: SpondylolisthesisRelevant Anatomy
text:
Intervertebral discs
A disc sits between each pair of adjacent vertebral bodies, including L5–S1. It contains a hydrated central nucleus pulposus within a fibrous annulus fibrosus. Together, these structures absorb axial and torsional loads while permitting motion.
With aging, the nucleus dehydrates and the annulus develops fissures. The resulting loss of disc height shifts load posteriorly onto the facet joints.



Source: Basic Medical Key.

title: SpondylolisthesisRelevant Anatomy
text:
Facet joints
The facet joints are paired synovial joints in which the inferior articular process above meets the superior articular process below. They are innervated by medial branches of the dorsal rami. Together with the disc, they resist forward translation.
Degeneration progresses from synovitis to cartilage loss, capsular laxity, subluxation, and articular-process hypertrophy. The resulting facet incompetence permits the slippage seen in degenerative spondylolisthesis.






NoteKey idea



Sagittally oriented facet joints are more permissive of forward slip and are a recognized anatomic risk factor for degenerative spondylolisthesis.

title: SpondylolisthesisRelevant Anatomy
text:
Pars interarticularis
The pars interarticularis is the narrow bony bridge linking the superior and inferior articular processes. It is a structural weak point of the posterior arch. Positioned between the anterior body load and posterior articular elements, it absorbs concentrated stress during repetitive extension and rotation, predisposing it to fatigue fracture, most often at L5.
A bilateral pars defect removes the bony restraint against forward slip, allowing progression to isthmic spondylolisthesis.

title: SpondylolisthesisRelevant Anatomy
text:
Spinal ligaments
The anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments, ligamentum flavum, and interspinous and supraspinous ligaments stabilize each functional spinal unit. With disc-height loss, the ligamentum flavum and posterior longitudinal ligament buckle and hypertrophy, encroaching on the canal. Interspinous bursitis is a recognized marker of developing degenerative spondylolisthesis.



Source: Basic Medical Key.

title: SpondylolisthesisRelevant Anatomy
text:
Neural elements
The spinal cord ends near L1; below this lies the cauda equina. Each lumbar root exits its foramen beneath the correspondingly numbered pedicle, such as the L2 root exiting below the L2 pedicle. This relationship provides the basis for correlating radicular symptoms with spinal level.
Slippage narrows the canal, lateral recesses, and foramina, compounding compression from disc protrusion, facet hypertrophy, and ligamentum flavum buckling.

title: SpondylolisthesisRelevant Anatomy
text:
Lumbosacral anatomy
The lower lumbar segments carry most of the axial load and are most affected by degeneration and slippage. The transition from the mobile lumbar spine to the fixed sacrum, together with the anteriorly inclined sacral endplate, generates shear that predisposes L5 to forward translation.
Isthmic slips predominate at L5–S1, while degenerative slips predominate at L4–L5.






TipPause and think



Why is the pars interarticularis particularly sensitive to developing spondylolysis?


Show answer

The pars sits at the junction between the anteriorly directed load of the vertebral body and the posterior articular processes, so it absorbs concentrated stress during repetitive extension and rotation. This makes it the structural weak point of the posterior arch and the site prone to fatigue fracture, most often at L5. Losing this bony bridge on both sides removes the restraint against forward slip.

title: SpondylolisthesisRelevant Anatomy
text:
Spinopelvic anatomy and alignment
Pelvic orientation drives sagittal balance and is measured on standing full-length lateral radiographs. Pelvic incidence (PI) is a fixed morphologic angle that governs pelvic tilt (PT) and sacral slope (SS):
\[\mathrm{PI} = \mathrm{PT} + \mathrm{SS}\]
Mean asymptomatic values are approximately 55° for PI, 41° for SS, and 13° for PT, with lumbar lordosis tracking these parameters. A high PI raises lumbosacral shear and is associated with both isthmic spondylolysis and the onset or progression of spondylolisthesis. Because abnormal parameters also affect fusion outcomes, they are integral to surgical planning.



Source: PMC.

title: SpondylolisthesisPathophysiology and Natural History
text:
Forward slip occurs when the posterior bony restraint against anterior shear at the lumbosacral junction fails, allowing one vertebra to translate on the one below. The mechanism differs by type.


A pars interarticularis defect, usually a fatigue fracture in genetically weak bone, removes the posterior restraint. A steep sacral slope and higher body weight increase shear across the sacral endplate.



Age-related degeneration of the disc and facet joints produces segmental instability that permits displacement over time. Degenerative change is theorized to progress through three stages: dysfunction, instability, and eventual restabilization through autofusion.
Predisposing anatomic features include horizontalization, or sagittal orientation, of the lamina and facets and high pelvic incidence, both of which increase shear across the segment.






TipPause and think



Why does isthmic spondylolisthesis usually occur at L5–S1, whereas degenerative spondylolisthesis usually occurs at L4–L5?


Show answer

The transition from the mobile lumbar spine to the fixed sacrum generates high shear at L5, predisposing it to pars fracture. Degenerative slip depends on disc and facet failure; L4–L5 is the most mobile segment, and its sagittal facets resist translation poorly once they degenerate.

title: SpondylolisthesisPathophysiology and Natural History
text:
Risk factors
Risk factors differ between the isthmic and degenerative forms.

Isthmic and pediatric disease

Repetitive hyperextension-rotation sports, including gymnastics, weightlifting, football, and diving
Male sex
Hereditary predisposition
Scoliosis
Spina bifida occulta



Degenerative disease

Older age
Higher body mass index
Facet osteoarthritis, particularly grade III or higher
Long-term physical labor
High pelvic incidence



Progression from lysis to listhesis

Disc degeneration, the most consistent predictor
High pelvic incidence







TipPause and think



An adolescent gymnast has activity-related low back pain that worsens with arching backward, and you notice tight hamstrings. What factors might raise suspicion for spondylolysis or a slip?


Show answer

Hyperextension and rotation load the pars, making fatigue fracture the leading concern. Extension-worsened pain points to a posterior-element source. Hamstring tightness may reflect a protective response to instability, with limited forward bending and a stiff, short-stride gait.

title: SpondylolisthesisPathophysiology and Natural History
text:
Slip progression and skeletal maturity
Isthmic slip progression concentrates during the adolescent growth spurt and largely halts at skeletal maturity. After maturity, the deformity is mechanically stable, with approximately 7% further slip reported in a long-term cohort. The dominant long-term problem becomes disc degeneration and low back pain rather than continued translation, and progression slows during each adult decade.

title: SpondylolisthesisIntroduction
text:
Spondylolisthesis is the forward slippage of one vertebra over the one directly below it, occurring most often at the lower lumbar levels. It is closely related to spondylolysis, a defect of the pars interarticularis; when such a defect is bilateral, the vertebra can slip forward, producing isthmic spondylolisthesis.
It is a common and clinically important cause of low back pain across all ages (reported prevalence approximately 4–6% in childhood and 5–10% in adults). In children and adolescents, it is a leading identifiable cause of back pain, especially in athletes who repeatedly hyperextend the spine; in older adults, the degenerative form contributes to back pain and lumbar spinal stenosis.






NoteBy the end of this module, you should be able to:




Define spondylolisthesis and use key terminology correctly, including spondylolysis, pars interarticularis, anterolisthesis, retrolisthesis, and spondyloptosis
Classify slips by etiology using the Wiltse-Newman classification and grade severity using Meyerding grades I–V
Explain the mechanisms, natural history, and risk factors distinguishing isthmic from degenerative disease
Recognize the clinical spectrum, from asymptomatic slips to back pain, radicular symptoms, and hamstring tightness
Perform a focused history and examination and build an appropriate differential
Select and interpret imaging and identify red flags warranting urgent referral
Outline nonoperative and operative management, including pediatric and high-grade considerations

title: SpondylolisthesisClinical Presentation
text: Most pars defects and slips are silent and are found incidentally. Slip magnitude correlates poorly with pain, and many patients, including those with isthmic disease, remain functional for years.

title: SpondylolisthesisClinical Presentation
text:
Low back pain
Mechanical pain is provoked by activity, prolonged standing, and lumbar extension and is relieved by rest or flexion. Isthmic disease and spondylolysis classically worsen with hyperextension and repetitive loading, particularly in adolescents and athletes.
Referred nonradicular pain to the buttock, hip, or posterior thigh may reflect facet or discogenic sources.

title: SpondylolisthesisClinical Presentation
text:
Radicular symptoms
Dermatomal leg pain can result from foraminal narrowing at the slip level. L5 symptoms are typical in isthmic L5–S1 slips, while L4 or L5 symptoms may occur in degenerative L4–L5 slips.
Degenerative slips with central or lateral-recess stenosis can cause neurogenic claudication: bilateral leg heaviness with walking or standing that is relieved by sitting or lumbar flexion. Patients may adopt a wide-based gait.

title: SpondylolisthesisClinical Presentation
text:
Neurologic deficits
Dermatomal sensory loss, myotomal weakness, and diminished reflexes can localize the affected level, although these findings are less common than pain alone.






ImportantRed flag



Cauda equina syndrome is rare but must be excluded. New urinary retention or incontinence, saddle anesthesia, reduced anal tone, or progressive or bilateral weakness require emergent MRI and urgent surgical referral.

title: SpondylolisthesisClinical Presentation
text:
Hamstring tightness
Hamstring tightness is a hallmark finding, especially in adolescents with higher-grade isthmic slips. It may present as reduced forward bending, limited straight-leg raise, and a stiff, short-stride gait. It is thought to be a protective response to instability rather than true neural tension and should raise suspicion in a young athlete with activity-related back pain.

title: SpondylolisthesisClinical Presentation
text:
Gait and postural abnormalities
Lumbosacral kyphosis and pelvic retroversion can produce a flattened lumbar contour, palpable step-off, shortened trunk, and, in severe L5–S1 slips, a crouched Phalen-Dickson gait. Degenerative stenosis instead tends to produce a forward-flexed posture and wide-based gait.



“Images of a ‘crouched’ gait (Phalen-Dickson sign), featuring excessive hip flexion, knee flexion, and ankle dorsiflexion.” Source: Pinnacle Orthocentre.

title: SpondylolisthesisClinical Presentation
text:
Physical examination
The examination emphasizes:

Inspection and palpation: Assess posture, lumbar contour, and a midline step-off; identify localized tenderness at the affected segment.
Range of motion: Assess flexion, extension, and rotation. Pain may be reproduced with lumbar hyperextension or, in athletes, single-leg hyperextension.
Neurologic testing: Test motor strength, sensation, and reflexes by myotome and dermatome. Perform a straight-leg raise when radicular tension signs are suspected.
Hamstring and gait assessment: Assess the popliteal angle and observe for a short-stride or crouched gait.

title: SpondylolisthesisClinical Presentation
text:
Differential diagnosis
The clinical picture overlaps with other mechanical and radicular causes of back and leg pain, several of which may coexist with a slip.

Lumbar disc herniation: Younger patients with acute, leg-dominant dermatomal pain that is worse with sitting and may be accompanied by a positive straight-leg raise.
Lumbar spinal stenosis: Older patients with neurogenic claudication and leg pain relieved by flexion; degenerative spondylolisthesis is itself a common cause.
Facet joint or discogenic pain: Axial pain with referral to the hip or thigh and no focal neurologic deficit.
Sacroiliac joint dysfunction: Buttock pain worse with sit-to-stand transitions, tenderness over the sacroiliac joint, and pain that does not localize above L5.
Hip pathology: Osteoarthritis or femoroacetabular impingement can cause groin or anterior-thigh pain with painful or limited hip rotation.







WarningCannot-miss diagnoses



Cauda equina syndrome, spinal epidural abscess, and spinal malignancy can mimic mechanical back pain. Fever, intravenous drug use, immunosuppression, markedly elevated ESR or CRP, age over 50, a history of cancer, unexplained weight loss, or night pain should prompt MRI and directed workup.


A structured diagnostic algorithm helps separate the majority of patients with nonspecific pain from the minority with serious or specific pathology.



Source: Cashin AG, Chou R, Weimer MB, McAuley JH. Low Back Pain: A Review. JAMA. 2026;336(2):144–158. JAMA.

title: SpondylolisthesisCase Example
text:
Becky P. is a 52-year-old woman presenting to clinic with a six-month history of gradually worsening lower back pain. She describes a deep ache across the lower back that is aggravated by prolonged standing, walking, and leaning backward, but improved by sitting or bending forward. She works as a nurse and spends most of her days on her feet, but has recently had difficulty keeping up because of aching and heaviness in her legs after walking for more than a few minutes. Stopping and leaning on a heavy object eases these episodes.






TipQuestion 1



What could these episodes of bilateral aching and heaviness indicate?


Show answer

Bilateral leg heaviness that occurs with walking or standing and eases with forward flexion is a sign of neurogenic claudication. This suggests central or lateral-recess narrowing, a common consequence of a degenerative slip.









TipQuestion 2



What specific history questions could you ask Becky to help characterize the pain and narrow the differential diagnosis?


Show answer


Onset: Was the onset insidious or sudden? Was there a recent fall or trauma?
Location and radiation: Where is the pain located? Does it radiate toward the buttock, leg, or thigh?
Neurologic symptoms: Is there numbness, weakness, foot drop, balance difficulty, or gait disturbance?
Red flags: Is there saddle anesthesia, urinary retention or incontinence, fecal incontinence, fever, intravenous drug use, a history of cancer, constitutional symptoms, chronic steroid use, or osteoporosis?










TipQuestion 3



You have ruled out red-flag symptoms such as saddle anesthesia and incontinence. Becky is otherwise healthy and denies fever, trauma, weight loss, or bladder or bowel changes. Which imaging study should you order first, and how should she be positioned?


Show answer

A standing, upright lateral radiograph of the lumbar spine is the initial test to detect and grade a slip. Upright positioning is important because a slip may reduce and appear normal when the patient is supine. Weight-bearing views reveal the true degree of translation. Anteroposterior and lateral views can also demonstrate the slip and the presence of a pars defect.









TipQuestion 4



A year later, Becky brings in her daughter, Maya, a 14-year-old competitive gymnast. Maya has had low back pain for several months, located in the lower back and noticeably worse with backbends and landings but improved by rest. She denies leg pain, numbness, weakness, or bladder or bowel symptoms. What is the most likely source of Maya’s pain, and how does it differ from her mother’s?


Show answer

Maya is a skeletally immature adolescent participating in a sport that demands repetitive lumbar hyperextension and rotation. Her pain is axial, activity-related, and relieved by rest, without radicular or red-flag features. This pattern points to spondylolysis, a stress injury of the pars interarticularis and the most common identifiable cause of low back pain in young athletes. It can progress to isthmic spondylolisthesis during the adolescent growth spurt.
By contrast, Becky’s pain reflects age-related disc and facet deterioration producing a degenerative slip and canal narrowing.









TipQuestion 5



Becky’s radiograph shows anterior slippage of L4 on L5, with the L4 body translated approximately one-third of the way forward over L5. How would you grade the severity of this slip?


Show answer

Severity is graded using the Meyerding scale from I to V. Translation of approximately one-third, or 25–50%, is a Meyerding grade II slip.

title: SpasticityManagement
text: Initial management of spasticity involves identifying the etiology. Management planning should include in-depth discussion of patient goals, support systems, and medical comorbidities.

title: SpasticityManagement
text:
Pharmacological Management

Baclofen
Baclofen is usually a first-line treatment for spasticity. It works as a pre- and postsynaptic GABA-B receptor agonist, restricting calcium influx and reducing excitatory signaling.
Oral baclofen is well absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract but has relatively limited penetration into the CNS. Adverse effects include weakness, fatigue, and sedation, and it should be used cautiously in older adults and in patients with renal impairment.


Intrathecal Baclofen
Intrathecal baclofen can be considered for severe generalized spasticity that does not respond adequately to, or is limited by adverse effects from, oral therapy.


Tizanidine
Tizanidine is an alpha-2 agonist that acts through presynaptic inhibition of motor neurons. It has a short half-life and therefore must be administered frequently to be effective. Adverse effects include sedation, hypotension, muscle weakness, and hallucinations.


Dantrolene
Dantrolene acts peripherally by inhibiting calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum in muscle. There have been reports of liver failure, including a few fatal cases, so it is not considered a first-line medication. Dantrolene does not selectively act on affected muscles and can cause generalized weakness.


Diazepam
Diazepam is a benzodiazepine that acts postsynaptically on GABA-A receptors and depresses CNS activity. It strongly induces sedation, which can make it useful at night. It tends to act on flexor responses and may be better suited to spinal spasticity than cerebral spasticity, although higher doses can suppress both. Adverse effects include dependence and tolerance.

title: SpasticityManagement
text:
Physiotherapy and Rehabilitation
Therapy should focus on impairments and function rather than solely on reducing spasticity. Interventions should strike a balance between movement and positioning.
Treatment options include:

Standing frames
Treadmill training, including body-weight-supported training when needed
Tilt tables
Active exercises
Passive movements
Twenty-four-hour positioning management
Splinting and orthotics
Dynamic stretching, including trunk twists, lunges, and leg swings




Example of an upper limb mobility and stretch exercise. Source: Manchester Physiotherapy.


Patient education on stretching and maintaining range of motion is important. Family members and caregivers should also be educated about positioning the patient in bed, a chair, or a wheelchair; checking for new wounds; avoiding noxious stimuli; and recognizing signs of discomfort or pain.
Home exercises that may help maintain range of motion include calf stretches, wall push-ups, standing and ambulation, unloaded cycling, and water-based exercises.

title: SpasticityManagement
text:
Interventional Management

Botulinum Toxin Injections
Botulinum toxin acts at the neuromuscular junction by blocking presynaptic acetylcholine release. The light chain enters the cell cytoplasm and cleaves SNAP-25, preventing vesicle fusion with the membrane and exocytosis of acetylcholine, resulting in chemical denervation.
Botulinum toxin is primarily used for focal or multifocal spasticity. The affected muscles may be identified using EMG, ultrasound, or electrical stimulation.
Contraindications to botulinum toxin injection include hypersensitivity and infection at the injection site. Special caution should be taken in patients with known neuromuscular disorders.


Functional Electrical Stimulation
Functional electrical stimulation may help increase plasticity in spinal cord circuitry.



Source: CESalud.

title: SpasticityIntroduction
text:
Spasticity is a velocity-dependent increase in muscle tone due to an exaggerated stretch reflex and is a component of the upper motor neuron syndrome.
This is a valuable topic to cover and is commonly seen in patients with neuromuscular conditions, particularly upper motor neuron lesions. Common etiologies include multiple sclerosis, stroke, spinal cord injury, and cerebral palsy. It is encountered by a wide range of specialties, including neurology, general internal medicine, family medicine, physical medicine, emergency medicine, and more.

title: SpasticityCase Example
text:
A 62-year-old man comes to the rehabilitation clinic four months after a left-sided ischemic stroke. He has right-sided weakness. Over the past few weeks, his right arm has become tight and curls up against his chest. He cannot open his right hand easily, and his wife has trouble cleaning his palm. He drags his right foot when he walks and has painful grabbing in the arm at night.
Past medical history includes high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, and atrial fibrillation treated with anticoagulation.



Right arm held with the elbow, wrist, and fingers bent and the forearm turned down.
When the elbow is straightened quickly, resistance increases and a catch is felt part-way through. Slow movement is easier.
Strength is weaker on the right, more so in the hand.
Reflexes are brisk on the right, with a few beats of ankle clonus and an upgoing right toe.
The joints can still be moved through a full range at rest, with no fixed stiffness yet.







TipQuestion 1



What is the best term for this increased tone, and which examination findings support it?


Show answer

The patient has spasticity. This is demonstrated by the velocity-dependent catch when the arm is passively moved quickly during the physical examination.









TipQuestion 2



What findings show this is part of the upper motor neuron syndrome?


Show answer

Weakness, brisk reflexes, clonus, a flexed arm posture, and an upgoing right toe are all signs of upper motor neuron syndrome.









TipQuestion 3



How do you distinguish spasticity from rigidity, dystonia, and a fixed contracture at the bedside? Which features does this patient have?


Show answer


Spasticity: Resistance is worse with fast stretch and shows a catch.
Rigidity: Resistance is similar at any speed, producing lead-pipe or cogwheel rigidity.
Dystonia: Sustained posturing or contraction occurs even at rest.
Fixed contracture: The joint cannot be moved through its full range at any speed.

The patient clearly has spasticity, as demonstrated by the velocity-dependent catch. His persistent flexed arm posture may also represent spastic dystonia, but the catch itself is a feature of spasticity.









TipQuestion 4



What would be the treatment plan for this patient?


Show answer

Physical rehabilitation would be the main treatment approach. Depending on the distribution and severity of symptoms, pharmacological agents and focal botulinum toxin treatment may also be considered. Intrathecal baclofen is an option for severe generalized spasticity that is inadequately controlled with, or limited by adverse effects from, oral therapy. Surgery, such as tendon lengthening, is reserved for severe cases that do not improve with more conservative treatments.

Weakness, brisk reflexes, clonus, a flexed arm posture, and an upgoing right toe are all signs of upper motor neuron syndrome.









TipQuestion 3



How do you distinguish spasticity from rigidity, dystonia, and a fixed contracture at the bedside? Which features does this patient have?


Show answer


Spasticity: Resistance is worse with fast stretch and shows a catch.
Rigidity: Resistance is similar at any speed, producing lead-pipe or cogwheel rigidity.
Dystonia: Sustained posturing or contraction occurs even at rest.
Fixed contracture: The joint cannot be moved through its full range at any speed.

The patient clearly has spasticity, as demonstrated by the velocity-dependent catch. His persistent flexed arm posture may also represent spastic dystonia, but the catch itself is a feature of spasticity.









TipQuestion 4



What would be the treatment plan for this patient?


Show answer

Physical rehabilitation would be the main treatment approach. Depending on the distribution and severity of symptoms, pharmacological agents and focal botulinum toxin treatment may also be considered. Intrathecal baclofen is an option for severe generalized spasticity that is inadequately controlled with, or limited by adverse effects from, oral therapy. Surgery, such as tendon lengthening, is reserved for severe cases that do not improve with more conservative treatments.

title: Lumbar Radicular PainRelevant Anatomy
text:
Radicular pain is easier to understand when you connect three pieces of anatomy:
The key idea is that radicular pain occurs when a spinal nerve root is irritated. When trying to understand a patient’s radicular pain, ask yourself two main questions:

title: Lumbar Radicular PainRelevant Anatomy
text:
The intervertebral disc
Intervertebral discs are fibrocartilaginous structures that sit between adjacent vertebral bodies. They essentially act like load-bearing cushions between the vertebrae.
Their major functions include:

Absorbing compressive forces
Distributing load across the spine
Allowing controlled movement between adjacent vertebrae
Helping maintain disc height and foraminal space

Each intervertebral disc has two major components:

The nucleus pulposus is the gelatinous central portion of the disc. It is rich in water and proteoglycans, which helps it absorb compression and distribute load.
The annulus fibrosus is the tougher outer ring of the disc. It is made of concentric collagen layers, which helps it resist tension, shearing, and rotational forces.

The interface between the disc and the adjacent vertebral body is called the cartilaginous endplate. The endplate is important because adult discs have very limited direct blood supply; instead, nutrients and waste products mainly move by diffusion across the endplate. This limited vascularity helps explain why discs have limited healing potential after injury.



Intervertebral disc between adjacent vertebrae, showing the nucleus pulposus and annulus fibrosus.



Source: Wikimedia Commons.

title: Lumbar Radicular PainRelevant Anatomy
text:
Disc loading and degeneration
Disc injury is often related to a combination of load, position, and movement.
Flexion increases pressure on the anterior part of the disc and can push disc material posteriorly. Rotation and twisting add shear forces across the annulus fibrosus. When these forces are combined, such as bending forward while twisting or lifting, the annulus is placed under even greater stress, further increasing the risk of injury. Common examples include deadlifting with poor form, shoveling, and lifting a heavy object while twisting.
In addition, discs can lose water and proteoglycan content over time. This reduces their ability to maintain disc height and distribute load, increasing stress on the annulus and contributing to bulging, tearing, and degenerative narrowing.



Intradiscal pressure is lowest when supine and highest when lifting a heavy object from a seated position.

title: Lumbar Radicular PainRelevant Anatomy
text:
Disc displacement terminology
Disc-related terms can be confusing because they sound similar. One helpful way to organize them is to first separate bulges from herniations.
A disc bulge is a broad-based extension of disc tissue beyond the normal disc margin. It involves a larger portion of the disc circumference, often described as more than 25%. A bulge can be:

Symmetric, where the disc extends outward relatively evenly
Asymmetric, where the broad-based extension is greater on one side

A disc herniation is more focal. It involves a smaller portion of the disc circumference, often described as less than 25%. Herniations are usually divided into:

Protrusion, where the displaced disc material remains broader at its base than at its outward extension.
Extrusion, where the displaced disc material extends farther outward and has a narrower connection to the parent disc.
Sequestration, where the displaced disc material completely separates from the parent disc.







TipPause and think



Which disc finding would you expect to have the worst prognosis: a bulge, protrusion, extrusion, or sequestration?


Show answer

Sequestration sounds the most severe because a fragment of disc material has separated from the parent disc. However, it does not automatically have the worst long-term pain prognosis. Sequestered fragments can sometimes be reabsorbed by the body over time.
By contrast, broad-based degenerative bulges may be less dramatic, but they can be frustrating because they are often more diffuse and may not provide a clear surgical or interventional target.
The main teaching point is that the most dramatic imaging term is not always the same as the most persistent or most treatable pain problem.






Visual representation of the different types of disc displacement.

title: Lumbar Radicular PainRelevant Anatomy
text:
How discs cause radicular pain
A disc herniation can cause radicular pain through two main mechanisms:

Mechanical compression
Chemical inflammation

Mechanical compression occurs when displaced disc material physically narrows the space around a nerve root. This can occur in the spinal canal, lateral recess, neural foramen, or extraforaminal region depending on the location of the herniation.
Chemical inflammation occurs because disc material and local inflammatory mediators can irritate the nerve root even when compression is not severe.
This explains why the degree of pain does not always perfectly match the size of the herniation seen on imaging. A large herniation may be minimally symptomatic if it is not irritating a clinically relevant nerve root, while a smaller herniation may cause severe radicular pain if it contacts and inflames the right nerve root.






NoteKey idea



Radicular pain is not always just a “pinched nerve.” It can involve both nerve root compression and nerve root inflammation.

title: Lumbar Radicular PainRelevant Anatomy
section: Spinal nerve roots and nerve root spaces
text:
Spinal nerve roots and nerve root spaces
The concept of traversing versus exiting nerve roots is high-yield because it explains why the level of a disc herniation does not always match the level of the affected nerve root. To better understand this we first need to define what determines whether a nerve root is traversing or exiting at a specific level, and what spaces these nerve roots pass through.
At a given lumbar disc level, there are usually two nerve roots to think about, and each travels through a different space:









Nerve root
Space
Definition




Exiting nerve root
Neural foramen
The nerve root that exits the spinal canal through the neural foramen at that disc level


Traversing nerve root
Lateral recess
The nerve root that continues downward through the lateral recess before exiting at the next level










NoteKey idea



A useful rule of thumb in the lumbar spine is that, at any given disc level, the exiting nerve root corresponds to the upper vertebra, while the traversing nerve root corresponds to the lower vertebra.
For example, at L4-L5, the L4 nerve root is the exiting nerve root because it exits below the L4 pedicle. The L5 nerve root is the traversing nerve root because it has not exited yet; instead, it continues downward through the lateral recess before exiting at the next level.





Example of exiting and traversing nerve roots including L3, L4, and L5 levels.



Source: TSRI eLibrary.

title: Lumbar Radicular PainRelevant Anatomy
text:
Herniation zones
The distinction between exiting and traversing nerve roots matters because the direction of a disc herniation helps determine which nerve root is affected. More lateral herniations can involve the neural foramen and affect the exiting nerve root, while more central or paracentral herniations can involve the lateral recess and affect the traversing nerve root.
The table below summarizes the main herniation zones and the nerve roots they are most likely to affect:








Herniation zone
Description




Central
Disc material herniates toward the middle of the spinal canal and may affect multiple nerve roots if the herniation is large.


Paracentral
Disc material herniates just lateral to the midline into the lateral recess and usually affects the traversing nerve root; at L4-L5, this is the L5 nerve root.


Foraminal
Disc material extends into the neural foramen and usually affects the exiting nerve root; at L4-L5, this is the L4 nerve root.


Extraforaminal
Disc material extends beyond the neural foramen and usually affects the exiting nerve root; at L4-L5, this is the L4 nerve root.










WarningRed flags



Central herniations are clinically important because a large central herniation can compress multiple nerve roots within the spinal canal. Severe compression of the cauda equina can cause bladder dysfunction, bowel dysfunction, saddle anesthesia, bilateral symptoms, or progressive neurologic deficits. These features require urgent assessment.








TipPause and think



At the L4-L5 disc level, which nerve root is more likely affected by a paracentral disc herniation?


Show answer

A paracentral disc herniation at L4-L5 usually affects the traversing L5 nerve root.
At this disc level, the L4 nerve root is the exiting root, while the L5 nerve root is still traveling downward through the lateral recess.

title: Lumbar Radicular PainCases
text: This section provides short practice cases to apply the radicular pain framework.

title: Lumbar Radicular PainCases
text:
Case 1: Acute leg-dominant pain
A 42-year-old patient presents with acute low back pain radiating down the posterolateral leg into the lateral foot after lifting a heavy object. The leg pain is more severe than the back pain and is described as sharp and electric. Symptoms worsen with sitting, coughing, and bending forward.
On exam, straight leg raise reproduces the typical leg pain. Ankle reflex is reduced on the affected side, and toe walking is mildly weak.






TipQuestion 1



Is this more consistent with axial low back pain or radicular pain?


Show answer

This is radicular pain, likely involving the S1 nerve root. The decisive clues are leg-dominant electric pain reaching the lateral foot, plus a reduced Achilles reflex and weak toe walking.









TipQuestion 2



Which nerve root is most likely involved?


Show answer

The S1 nerve root is most likely involved. The lateral-foot sensory distribution, reduced Achilles reflex, and weak toe walking all localize to S1.









TipQuestion 3



Are there any red flags that require urgent imaging?


Show answer

No urgent imaging is required from the information given. The weakness is mild and not described as progressive, and there are no cauda equina or systemic red flags. Reassess urgently if weakness progresses or bowel, bladder, saddle, or bilateral symptoms develop.









TipQuestion 4



What would be a reasonable initial management plan?


Show answer

Start with conservative, function-focused care: stay active as tolerated, use appropriate analgesia, and begin physiotherapy guided by symptom response. The goal is to maintain function while monitoring for neurologic worsening.

title: Lumbar Radicular PainCases
text:
Case 2: Persistent radicular pain
A 58-year-old patient has six months of right leg-dominant pain radiating from the buttock into the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot. The pain is burning and electric. It has not improved despite medications and physiotherapy. MRI shows right L4-L5 lateral recess stenosis affecting the traversing L5 nerve root.






TipQuestion 1



Does the imaging finding match the clinical pattern?


Show answer

Yes. Right L4-L5 lateral recess stenosis affects the traversing L5 nerve root, which matches the patient’s pain in the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot.









TipQuestion 2



Which nerve root is most likely affected?


Show answer

The L5 nerve root is most likely affected. At the L4-L5 level, L5 is the traversing root, so lateral recess pathology at this level commonly affects L5.









TipQuestion 3



What interventional pain option could be considered?


Show answer

A right L5 transforaminal epidural steroid injection is a reasonable option. The symptoms, suspected root, and MRI target all line up: right L5-pattern pain with right L4-L5 lateral recess stenosis affecting the traversing L5 root.









TipQuestion 4



When would surgical referral be reasonable?


Show answer

Surgical referral is reasonable if symptoms remain severe and function-limiting despite appropriate nonoperative management, because there is a concordant, surgically treatable lesion. It becomes urgent if progressive significant weakness or cauda equina symptoms develop.

title: Lumbar Radicular PainInvestigations
text: Most acute radicular pain does not require immediate imaging. In fact, many cases improve with just conservative management alone. However, there are specific instances where further investigation can or should be considered, depending on the severity of symptoms.

title: Lumbar Radicular PainInvestigations
text:
When imaging is not indicated
In a patient with acute radicular pain, no red flags, and no progressive or severe neurologic deficit, immediate imaging is often not needed.
This is because early imaging may show disc bulges, degenerative changes, or other abnormalities that are not necessarily causing the patient’s symptoms. Imaging too early can therefore paradoxically make management less clear rather than more clear.
Initial management is instead usually guided by:

Severity of pain
Functional limitation
Neurologic examination
Presence or absence of red flags
Response to conservative care over time







NoteKey idea



Imaging should be ordered when the result is likely to change management, not simply because radicular pain is present.

title: Lumbar Radicular PainInvestigations
text:
When imaging is indicated
Imaging is more useful when symptoms are:

Persistent despite appropriate conservative management
Severe or function-limiting
Progressive
Associated with objective neurologic deficit
Associated with red flags
Being evaluated for an epidural steroid injection or surgical referral

title: Lumbar Radicular PainInvestigations
text:
Choice of imaging
MRI lumbar spine is the preferred imaging test when imaging is indicated. MRI shows many soft tissue structures with great resolution, including the discs, nerve roots, spinal canal, lateral recesses, and neural foramina.
For routine lumbar radicular pain, MRI without contrast is usually sufficient. Contrast is generally reserved for situations where there is concern for infection, malignancy, inflammatory disease, or post-operative scar versus recurrent disc herniation.







Investigation
Role




MRI lumbar spine
Best test for disc herniation, stenosis, and nerve root compression


CT lumbar spine
Useful if MRI is contraindicated or unavailable; better for bony anatomy


X-ray
Useful for quick assessment for alignment, spondylolisthesis, fracture, or degenerative change, but does not show nerve compression well






MRI of the lumbar spine, showing a herniated and bulging disc.





CT of the lumbar spine, useful for more detailed assessment of bony anatomy.



Source: NCCommons / Radiopaedia.




X-ray of the lumbar spine, useful for a quick screen of degenerative changes.



Source: NCCommons / Radiopaedia.

title: Lumbar Radicular PainInvestigations
section: Matching imaging to the clinical picture
text:
Matching imaging to the clinical picture
Imaging findings must always be matched to the patient’s symptoms and exam.
Disc bulges, degenerative changes, and stenosis are common in asymptomatic people. An MRI abnormality is only clinically meaningful if it fits the pain distribution, neurologic findings, and suspected root level.
For example, an L4-L5 paracentral disc herniation may be clinically meaningful if the patient has L5-pattern leg pain, weakness of great toe extension, or other findings that fit L5 involvement. The same imaging finding may be less meaningful if the patient’s symptoms point to a different level or a different diagnosis.






TipPause and think



Our patient has right-sided L5-pattern radicular pain. MRI shows a small right paracentral L4-L5 disc herniation and a larger left-sided disc bulge at another level. Which finding is more clinically relevant?


Show answer

The right paracentral L4-L5 disc herniation is more clinically relevant because it matches his right-sided L5-pattern symptoms.
The larger left-sided disc bulge may be incidental if it does not match the clinical pattern.









NoteKey idea



Do not treat the MRI in isolation. Treat the patient and use imaging to support the clinical diagnosis.

title: Lumbar Radicular PainInvestigations
text:
Role of EMG/NCS
EMG/NCS can help when the diagnosis is uncertain or when there is disagreement between symptoms, exam, and imaging.
It may be useful to:

Support a diagnosis of radiculopathy
Identify chronic or active denervation
Distinguish radiculopathy from peripheral neuropathy or plexopathy
Clarify the affected root level when the clinical picture is unclear

EMG/NCS is mainly a test of nerve function. It is more useful for confirming radiculopathy than for confirming radicular pain alone. It is also less useful very early in the course because denervation changes may take time to appear.



EMG/NCS testing of the lower limb, showing the surface electrodes and needle electrode used for electromyography.

title: Lumbar Radicular PainClinical Presentation
text:
Lumbar radicular pain usually presents with leg-dominant symptoms.
Clinically, the stepwise approach is:

title: Lumbar Radicular PainClinical Presentation
text:
Timeline
The first distinction to make is the duration of symptoms.
Acute lumbar radicular pain often presents suddenly, especially after a lifting, bending, or twisting movement. In younger and middle-aged patients, this raises suspicion for an acute disc herniation irritating a nerve root.
Chronic lumbar radicular pain is usually more gradual or recurrent. In older patients, this is often related to degenerative narrowing of the lateral recess or neural foramen, which can irritate or compress the nerve root over time.

title: Lumbar Radicular PainClinical Presentation
text:
Terminology
Neuropathic pain is a broad term that refers to pain generated from injury or disease affecting any part of the nervous system including nerves, nerve roots, the spinal cord, or the brain.
Patients may describe this sort of pain as:

Shooting
Burning
Electric
Sharp
Stabbing
Traveling down the leg

Radicular pain specifically refers to pain generated by injury or disease to a nerve root.






NoteKey idea



Radicular pain is a subtype of neuropathic pain.
Therefore, all radicular pain is neuropathic pain, but not all neuropathic pain is radicular pain.


Radiculopathy is also related, but distinct. Remember that pain is a subjective experience, so patients can have radicular pain without objective neurologic deficits. Radiculopathy, on the other hand, implies that the nerve root is not only irritated, but also functionally impaired, leading to objecitve findings on examination.






NoteKey idea



Radicular pain describes the subjective pain pattern. Radiculopathy describes objective nerve root dysfunction.









Term
Meaning




Radicular pain
Pain generated by irritation or inflammation of a spinal nerve root


Neuropathic pain
Pain caused by injury or disease affecting the somatosensory nervous system


Radiculopathy
Objective nerve root dysfunction, such as weakness, sensory loss, or reflex change

title: Lumbar Radicular PainClinical Presentation
text:
Symptom pattern
Symptoms may worsen with activities that increase nerve root tension or intradiscal pressure, such as:

Sitting
Bending forward
Coughing
Sneezing
Valsalva

Depending on the cause, symptoms may also worsen with standing or extension. This is especially relevant when foraminal stenosis is the main driver.






TipPause and think



In the opening case, the patient develops acute radiating leg pain after deadlifting. Which movement would you expect to aggravate his pain more: lumbar flexion or lumbar extension?


Show answer

Lumbar flexion would be more likely to aggravate his pain.
Because the symptoms are acute and started during lifting, an acute disc herniation is higher on the differential. Disc-related radicular pain is often worsened by flexion, sitting, bending forward, coughing, or Valsalva.
By contrast, pain from degenerative foraminal stenosis is often worse with lumbar extension, because extension can further narrow the neural foramen.

title: Lumbar Radicular PainClinical Presentation
text:
Dermatomes
A dermatome is an area of skin supplied mainly by one spinal nerve root.
In radicular pain, the pain or sensory symptoms may follow a dermatomal pattern. For example, irritation of the L5 nerve root often causes symptoms that travel down the lateral leg toward the dorsum of the foot.







Nerve root
Broad sensory distribution




L2
Anterior upper thigh


L3
Anterior thigh and medial knee


L4
Medial leg and medial ankle


L5
Lateral leg, dorsum of foot, great toe


S1
Posterior leg, lateral foot, sole


S2
Posterior thigh and upper posterior calf






Dermatomes of the lower limbs.

title: Lumbar Radicular PainClinical Presentation
text:
Myotomes and reflexes
A myotome is a group of muscles supplied mainly by one spinal nerve root.
Myotomes help identify whether radicular pain has progressed to radiculopathy. Weakness in a myotomal pattern suggests that the affected nerve root is not only irritated, but also functionally impaired.








Root
Motor findings
Reflex




L3
Hip flexion, knee extension
Patellar may be reduced


L4
Knee extension, ankle dorsiflexion
Patellar


L5
Great toe extension, ankle dorsiflexion, hip abduction
No reliable reflex


S1
Plantarflexion, toe walking
Achilles









TipPause and think



The patient from the earlier case now seems to have weakness with great toe extension on exam. Which nerve root would this make you most concerned about?


Show answer

Great toe extension is commonly used to assess the L5 nerve root. Weakness here would make L5 radiculopathy more likely.

title: Lumbar Radicular PainClinical Presentation
text:
Provocative tests
Provocative tests can support the diagnosis by increasing tension on irritated nerve roots. A positive result on these tests increases your suspicion for lumbar radicular pain.
Straight leg raise (Lasègue test). With the patient lying supine, passively raise the straightened leg to about 30–70° and assess whether this reproduces radiating leg pain. A positive result suggests lower lumbar radicular irritation, especially involving L5 or S1.
Crossed straight leg raise. Raise the unaffected leg and assess whether this reproduces radicular pain in the symptomatic leg. This test is less sensitive but more specific for disc herniation.



Example of how to do the straight leg raise test.


Bragard test. After a positive straight leg raise, slightly lower the leg until pain improves, then dorsiflex the ankle to see if radicular pain returns. This supports neural tension or lower lumbar radicular irritation.



Example of how to do the Bragard test.


Slump test. With the patient seated, flex the spine and neck, extend the knee, and dorsiflex the ankle to tension the neural system. A positive result suggests neural tension or radicular irritation.



Example of how to do the slump test.


Femoral stretch test. With the patient prone or side-lying, extend the hip and flex the knee to stretch the femoral nerve. A positive result suggests upper lumbar radicular irritation, especially involving L2 to L4.



Example of how to do the femoral nerve stretch test.








CautionWord of caution



Be careful not to misinterpret hamstring tightness or other forms of non-radicular discomfort as a positive test. Hamstring tightness is often felt as a localized pulling, stretching, or aching sensation in the back of the thigh, without the patient’s usual electric or shooting pain traveling below the knee. A positive result specifically refers to reproduction of the patient’s typical radiating leg pain, which often travels into the calf, foot, or toes.








TipPause and think



On exam, the patient has pain radiating down the leg during a straight leg raise, but no pain during the femoral stretch test. What does this suggest?


Show answer

This pattern supports lower lumbar nerve root irritation, especially involving the L5 or S1 nerve roots.
A positive straight leg raise is more consistent with lower lumbar radicular pain, while the femoral stretch test is more useful for upper lumbar nerve root irritation, especially L2 to L4.

title: Lumbar Radicular PainClinical Presentation
text:
Red flag features
Red flag features should be screened for because not all radiating leg pain is benign.
They can be remembered using the NIFTI mnemonic:







Category
Features




Neurologic
New urinary retention or overflow incontinence, saddle anesthesia, bilateral severe neurologic symptoms, or progressive motor weakness


Infection
Fever, immunosuppression, IV drug use, or other concern for infection


Fracture
Significant trauma


Tumour
History of malignancy, unexplained weight loss, or severe unremitting night pain


Inflammation
Onset before age 45 with prolonged morning stiffness, improvement with exercise, or pain that does not improve with rest

title: Pain FundamentalsSensitization
text:
Sensitization refers to increased responsiveness of the pain system. In simple terms, the nervous system becomes easier to activate and may produce a stronger, more widespread, or more persistent pain response than expected.
This is clinically important because pain severity does not always match the amount of tissue damage. In some patients, pain may be amplified by changes in the peripheral or central nervous system, rather than being explained only by one injured structure.
The two major forms are:

title: Pain FundamentalsSensitization
text:
Peripheral sensitization
Peripheral sensitization occurs when peripheral nociceptors become more sensitive after tissue injury or inflammation.
Normally, nociceptors require a certain level of stimulation before they fire. With peripheral sensitization, this threshold decreases, meaning a smaller stimulus can trigger pain. The same stimulus may also produce a larger pain response than it normally would.
This is often driven by inflammatory mediators released around the injured tissue, such as prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, cytokines, substance P, CGRP, and nerve growth factor. Local chemical changes, such as increased acidity or ATP release from damaged cells, can also contribute. These mediators make nociceptors easier to activate.
Clinically, this helps explain why an injured area becomes tender, sore, and more painful to touch or movement. For example, after a sunburn, light pressure on the burned skin may feel much more painful than usual.

title: Pain FundamentalsSensitization
text:
Central sensitization
Central sensitization occurs when neurons in the spinal cord and brain become more excitable and amplify incoming pain signals.
This can happen after repeated or prolonged nociceptive input. At the dorsal horn, increased release of excitatory neurotransmitters such as glutamate, substance P, and CGRP can increase the responsiveness of second-order neurons. Activation of NMDA receptors is especially important because it can make these neurons more excitable over time. At the same time, reduced inhibitory signaling through neurotransmitters such as GABA and glycine can further increase pain transmission.
As a result, the central nervous system may become more responsive to incoming signals, so pain can become more widespread, more persistent, or disproportionate to the original injury.
Clinical features can include:

Allodynia
Secondary hyperalgesia
Pain spread beyond the original injury site
Widespread pain
Persistent pain after tissue healing
Pain that seems disproportionate to ongoing tissue findings

Persistent pain can also disrupt sleep, mood, activity, and function. These factors can then feed back into the pain system and further increase pain sensitivity, creating a cycle that becomes harder to reverse over time.

title: Pain FundamentalsSensitization
text:
Case example
Consider a patient who initially has focal medial knee pain after a local knee injury.
Early on, the pain may be mostly localized to the medial knee and driven by nociceptive input from injured or inflamed tissue. If pain persists, the surrounding tissues may become more sensitive, and the patient may begin to report pain around the whole knee rather than only at the original site.
Over time, ongoing nociceptive input and reduced activity, poor sleep, fear of movement, or distress can contribute to broader pain amplification. The patient may develop diffuse sensitivity around the knee, pain with normally tolerable movements, or pain that feels disproportionate to the original tissue findings.
This example illustrates how pain can progress from a more localized nociceptive problem toward a more sensitized pain state.

title: Pain FundamentalsSensitization
text:
Comparison table








Feature
Peripheral sensitization
Central sensitization




Main site
Peripheral nociceptors
Spinal cord and brain


Main process
Nociceptors become easier to activate
CNS amplifies incoming pain signals


Typical pattern
Tenderness and increased pain at the injury site
Pain spread, allodynia, disproportionate or persistent pain


Hyperalgesia pattern
Primary hyperalgesia, meaning increased pain sensitivity at the site of injury
Secondary hyperalgesia, meaning increased pain sensitivity outside the original injury site


Example
Sunburned skin feels very painful to light pressure
Pain sensitivity spreads beyond the injured area or persists after tissue healing






Peripheral sensitization occurs at the level of nociceptors, while central sensitization reflects amplification within the spinal cord and brain.

title: Pain FundamentalsSensitization
text:
Clinical takeaway
One goal of early pain management is to reduce the chance that acute pain becomes persistent and sensitized.
This does not mean all pain can be prevented from becoming chronic. However, timely education, appropriate activity, symptom control, sleep support, functional rehabilitation, and attention to psychosocial contributors can help reduce persistent nociceptive input and maintain function.






TipPause and think



Why might early active management be preferable to prolonged rest after many painful musculoskeletal injuries?


Show answer

Prolonged rest can contribute to deconditioning, fear of movement, sleep disruption, and reduced function. Early active management aims to control symptoms while helping the patient maintain safe movement and gradually return to normal activity.
This can reduce persistent nociceptive input and may lower the risk of pain becoming more sensitized over time.

Nerve injury is important in pain medicine because damage to the somatosensory nervous system can produce neuropathic pain.
Nerve injury can affect different parts of a nerve, including:
The severity of injury influences both recovery potential and the likelihood of persistent symptoms.

title: Pain FundamentalsNerve Injury
text:
Basic nerve structure
A peripheral nerve is more than just a bundle of axons. It also has supporting connective tissue layers.
This matters because nerve recovery depends not only on whether the axon is injured, but also on whether the surrounding scaffold remains intact.







Structure
Simple role




Myelin
Insulates axons and helps signals travel quickly


Axon
Carries the nerve signal


Endoneurium
Connective tissue around individual nerve fibers


Perineurium
Connective tissue around a fascicle, or bundle of nerve fibers


Epineurium
Outer connective tissue layer around the whole nerve






Peripheral nerve structure showing the axon and surrounding endoneurium, perineurium, and epineurium.



Source: Tortora & Derrickson, Principles of Anatomy & Physiology.

title: Pain FundamentalsNerve Injury
text:
Seddon classification
The Seddon classification is a simple way to categorize peripheral nerve injury.








Injury type
Meaning
Recovery potential

Conduction block without axonal disruption
Best


Axonotmesis
Axon is disrupted, but connective tissue framework is at least partly preserved
Possible through regeneration


Neurotmesis

Worst



In practical terms:

Neurapraxia is usually the most reversible because the axon remains intact.
Axonotmesis can recover if the axon regenerates along a preserved scaffold.
Neurotmesis has the poorest recovery because nerve continuity is disrupted.

title: Pain FundamentalsNerve Injury
text:
Why nerve injury can hurt
Nerve injury can cause abnormal signaling within the somatosensory system.
This may lead to:

Spontaneous pain
Burning pain
Electric or shooting pain
Dysesthesia
Allodynia
Hyperalgesia
Pain in an area with reduced sensation

One clinically important feature of neuropathic pain is that patients can have both reduced sensation and pain in the same region. This may seem contradictory at first, but it reflects abnormal nerve function rather than normal tissue warning signals.
Injured nerves may generate ectopic discharges, become more sensitive to stimulation, or form painful neuroma-like changes after trauma or surgery. These abnormal signals can then be amplified by peripheral or central sensitization.

title: Pain FundamentalsNerve Injury
text:
Regeneration and recurrent pain
If the connective tissue framework is preserved, axons may regenerate over time.
This is clinically important because some pain procedures intentionally interrupt nerve signaling without completely destroying the nerve framework. Pain relief may occur, but symptoms can recur if the nerve regenerates.
This concept helps explain why treatments such as radiofrequency ablation can provide meaningful relief for months, but may not be permanent.

title: Pain FundamentalsIntroduction
text:
Pain is one of the most important concepts in clinical medicine. It is common, personal, and often multifactorial. Understanding pain requires more than simply identifying tissue damage because pain is shaped by the peripheral nervous system, the central nervous system, as well as the broader biological, psychological, and social context of the patient.
This module is designed to be the first that students will complete in this series of pain-related modules. The goal is to introduce the core language and physiology needed to understand pain presentations in a structured way, before delving into clinical cases.
Estimated time: 50–65 minutes






NoteBy the end of this module, you should be comfortable with:




Defining pain and distinguishing it from nociception
Using common pain terminology correctly
Differentiating nociceptive, neuropathic, and nociplastic pain
Describing basic pain pathways from peripheral stimulus to cortical perception
Understanding peripheral and central sensitization
Explaining how pain can be modulated by the nervous system
Recognizing basic patterns of nerve injury
Understanding the basic rationale behind radiofrequency ablation

The intervertebral disc is a fibrocartilaginous joint between adjacent vertebral bodies that works as a pressurized cushion: it absorbs compression, distributes load, permits controlled motion, and maintains disc height. The three main components of the intervertebral disc are as follows:









Structure
Composition
Function




Nucleus pulposus
Gel-like core, 70-90% water, rich in aggrecan
Negative charge draws in water, generating the hydrostatic pressure that resists axial load


Annulus fibrosus
Concentric collagen lamellae angled in alternating directions
Contains the pressurized nucleus and converts compression into circumferential “hoop” tension, resisting bending and twisting

title: Discogenic PainRelevant Anatomy
text:
Pain Pathway Review
Before delving further, let’s quickly review how a pain signal travels from the spine to the brain. Once nociceptors in the outer annulus and endplate are activated, the signal follows a three-neuron relay to the brain.

First-order neuron. Nociceptors in the disc are activated, and the signal travels along slow A-delta and C fibers through the sinuvertebral nerve. The first-order neuron cell body lies in the dorsal root ganglion, and its central process enters the dorsal horn of the spinal cord.
Synapse and crossover in the dorsal horn. In the dorsal horn, the first-order neuron synapses on a second-order projection neuron. The signal can be amplified or dampened at this point before the second-order neuron crosses to the opposite side of the spinal cord.
Second-order neuron. After crossing, the second-order neuron ascends in the spinothalamic tract within the anterolateral spinal cord and travels to the thalamus, the brain’s main sensory relay station.
Third-order neuron. The third-order neuron carries the signal from the thalamus to the primary somatosensory cortex, where the pain reaches conscious perception.

Nociceptive information ascends through parallel pathways. The lateral spinothalamic pathway projects through the thalamus to the somatosensory cortex and helps encode the location, intensity, and duration of pain. Medial pathways, including the spinoreticular and spinomesencephalic tracts, project through brainstem, thalamic, and limbic structures and contribute to the emotional, unpleasant quality of pain.

title: Discogenic PainRelevant Anatomy
text:
Blood and Neural Supply
The intervertebral disc is the largest avascular structure in the body. Blood vessels reach only the outer rim of the annulus fibrosus, while the nucleus pulposus and inner annulus have no direct blood supply of their own. Instead, the disc is nourished by slow diffusion of nutrients and metabolic waste across the cartilaginous endplates, which lie between the disc and the small vessels of the adjacent vertebral bodies.
Sensory nerve fibers normally penetrate only the outermost layers of the annulus fibrosus, while the inner annulus and the entire nucleus pulposus remain nerve-free. Because pain requires functioning nociceptors, a structurally intact disc is inherently a poor generator of pain. Yet, degeneration can advance silently for years, causing pain once the disc becomes disrupted.



Source: Journal of Cellular Physiology.


The disc’s sensory supply is central to understanding discogenic pain, because pain is generated by a small set of specific nerves that are also the targets of diagnostic blocks and ablation. Two are most important: the sinuvertebral nerve (SVN), which supplies the disc itself, and its branch, the basivertebral nerve (BVN), which supplies the vertebral endplate.

Sinuvertebral Nerve (SVN)
The SVN is the disc’s main sensory nerve. The SVN reaches the disc and posterior longitudinal ligament by looping back through the intervertebral foramen. Its innervation overlaps across levels, with each posterior disc supplied both by its own SVN and by the SVN from the level below, an arrangement that helps explain why discogenic pain tends to be diffuse and poorly localized. It also preferentially innervates the posterior and posterolateral annulus, precisely the region where painful annular fissures concentrate.


Basivertebral Nerve (BVN)
A branch of the SVN, the BVN is the sensory nerve of the vertebral endplate and carrier of “vertebrogenic” pain. It re-enters the vertebral body through the basivertebral foramen and runs to a central trunk (~30-50% into the body) that splits toward the superior and inferior endplates, the target of basivertebral nerve ablation.



Source: Basivertebral Nerve Ablation.

title: Discogenic PainPathophysiology
text: Discogenic pain reflects a paradox: the disc is normally the largest avascular, nearly aneural structure in the body, yet it can become a potent pain generator. This happens in sequential stages, each building on the last: degeneration disrupts the matrix, annular fissures open pathways for nerves and vessels to grow inward, inflammation takes hold, and the ingrown nerve endings become sensitized.

title: Discogenic PainPathophysiology
text:
1. Degeneration
With aging, repetitive load, genetic predisposition, and poor nutrition, the disc starts breaking itself down faster than it can rebuild:

Cells die off and stop making aggrecan (the molecule that holds water), while enzymes (MMPs, ADAMTS) chew up the existing matrix.
Uneven load stresses the tough outer ring (annulus), creating cracks called annular fissures, leading to discogenic pain.

This structural failure within the disc is sometimes termed internal disc disruption and can occur without disc herniation or nerve root compression.

title: Discogenic PainPathophysiology
text:
2. Nerve and Vessel Ingrowth
In a healthy disc, sensory nerves are confined to the outer edge of the annulus. Annular fissures serve as conduits, allowing small blood vessels and nociceptive fibers (C and A-delta) to extend into the deeper, previously insensate regions of the disc. With pain-sensing endings now embedded within the disc, mechanical loads that a normal disc would never register are perceived as pain.

title: Discogenic PainPathophysiology
text:
3. Inflammation
Once the disc’s internal environment is disrupted, resident disc cells and infiltrating macrophages release inflammatory mediators that sustain a self-perpetuating cycle:

Predominantly IL-1β and TNF-α (along with IL-6), which accelerate matrix breakdown and recruit additional immune cells.
These mediators also upregulate NGF, directly linking inflammation to further nerve ingrowth and nerve activation.
Accumulating metabolic waste lowers the local pH, and this acidic environment directly irritates the ingrown nerve endings.

title: Discogenic PainPathophysiology
text:
4. Sensitization
Persistent chemical and mechanical irritation lowers the firing threshold of these new nerve endings, so that even normal movement provokes pain (peripheral sensitization). Over time, the spinal cord and brain amplify the incoming signals (central sensitization), which explains why discogenic pain can become chronic and diffuse even when the structural disc damage is modest.

title: Discogenic PainInvestigations
text:
Choice of Imaging
MRI is the study of choice for evaluating the disc when imaging is indicated. Plain radiographs are a reasonable initial step to screen for fracture, malignancy, or spondylolisthesis. CT is reserved for patients who cannot undergo MRI.







Investigation
Role




MRI lumbar spine
Preferred study for the disc; depicts nucleus, annulus, endplates, and neural structures, and reveals degenerative and inflammatory changes that support a discogenic source


CT lumbar spine
Alternative when MRI cannot be done; superior for bony detail but less reliable for disc and soft-tissue evaluation


X-ray
Quick screen for alignment, spondylolisthesis, fracture, and disc-space narrowing, but cannot image the disc or show its pain-generating features



Imaging in suspected discogenic pain serves two purposes: excluding other pathology (fracture, tumor, infection, nerve root compression) and identifying candidate painful levels. The central caveat is that degenerative findings are common in people without pain, so no imaging finding is diagnostic on its own and all findings must be correlated with symptoms.

title: Discogenic PainInvestigations
text:
Pfirrmann Grade
The earliest and most consistent MRI marker is loss of the normal bright T2 nucleus signal, with progressive darkening, loss of nucleus-annulus distinction, and disc-height collapse. This is graded I-V on the Pfirrmann scale; grades IV-V correlate best with a positive discogram.



Source: ResearchGate.

title: Discogenic PainInvestigations
text:
High-Intensity Zones (HIZ)
A high-intensity zone is a focal bright T2 signal within the posterior annulus fibrosus, distinct from the nucleus, and represents a fluid- or granulation-tissue-filled annular fissure that has reached the outer, innervated annulus. When present, an HIZ is a reasonably specific marker of a painful posterior annular tear: HIZ discs frequently reproduce concordant pain at discography, and the finding correlates with grade IV-V degeneration and endplate changes. However, it is important to note that HIZs have low sensitivity, so their absence does not exclude a discogenic source, and HIZs can also appear in asymptomatic people.



A T2W MRI depicting a high-intensity zone (HIZ) in the posterior annulus of the intervertebral disc. Source: Radiopaedia.

title: Discogenic PainInvestigations
text:
Modic (Endplate) Changes and Vertebrogenic Pain
Modic changes are signal changes in the vertebral bone next to the endplate, and they mark the closely related “vertebrogenic” phenotype, where the endplate rather than the disc is the pain source. There are three types: Type 1 (edema; dark T1, bright T2) is the type most consistently linked to low back pain, Type 2 (fatty; bright T1 and T2) is more chronic, and Type 3 (sclerotic; dark on both) is least associated with pain.

title: Discogenic PainInvestigations
text:
Provocation Discography
Provocation discography remains the only test that directly probes whether a specific disc reproduces the patient’s pain, and it is considered the reference standard for internal disc disruption, though it is invasive and controversial. Under fluoroscopy, contrast is injected into the suspect disc and at least one adjacent control disc. The test is positive when injecting the suspect disc reproduces the patient’s concordant pain (>=6/10 at low pressure) while the control disc stays painless. A post-procedure CT can then assess and grade annular fissuring.






NoteKey idea



A positive result needs both concordant pain in the suspect disc and a painless control disc. Pain alone, without a negative control, does not confirm a discogenic source.

title: Discogenic PainClinical Presentation
text: A practical way to approach a patient is to ask three questions in sequence:

title: Discogenic PainClinical Presentation
text:
Timeline
The tempo of symptoms shapes the differential. An acute flare, often triggered by a lift, bend, or twist, tends to occur in younger and middle-aged adults and reflects an annular fissure or early internal disruption. A chronic or relapsing course, with recurrent bouts of axial pain over months to years, is more typical of established degenerative disc disease.

title: Discogenic PainClinical Presentation
text:
Symptom Pattern
The hallmark is intolerance of positions and activities that raise intradiscal pressure:

Prolonged sitting and standing up from a seated position
Forward bending and sustained flexion (leaning over a sink, tying shoes)
Coughing, sneezing, or straining (Valsalva)







NoteKey idea



The “worse with sitting and flexion, better lying flat” pattern is the most recognizable signature and helps separate discogenic pain from facet-mediated pain, which typically worsens with extension, standing, and walking.








TipPause and think



A 40-year-old office worker reports midline low back pain that is worse with prolonged sitting and forward bending, and eased by standing and walking. There is no leg pain and the neurologic exam is normal. Why does this pattern point toward a discogenic source rather than facet-mediated pain?


Show answer

Discogenic pain is classically axial and midline, worsened by flexion-based, disc-loading activities such as sitting and bending forward, since these positions raise intradiscal pressure. Facet-mediated pain, by contrast, tends to produce paraspinal rather than midline tenderness and is typically worse with extension and rotation. The absence of leg pain and a normal neurologic exam also argue against a radicular source.

title: Discogenic PainClinical Presentation
text:
Physical Exam
Unlike radicular pain, where provocative maneuvers stretch an irritated nerve root, discogenic pain has no equivalent set of nerve-tension tests. The disc is a deep axial structure, so bedside “provocation” instead relies on loading the disc mechanically and observing pain behavior.









Test
How it is performed
Suggests




Centralization
With the patient standing or prone, have them perform repeated end-range lumbar movements (usually extension, e.g. prone press-ups) while tracking where the pain is felt
A discogenic source if referred buttock/thigh pain migrates toward the midline


Directional preference
Test repeated movements in several directions to find one that reduces or centralizes pain
A discogenic source; specific but insensitive; rules in rather than out


Axial loading/sustained flexion
Load the flexed spine with prolonged sitting, forward bending, or axial compression
Mechanical disc source if concordant midline axial pain is reproduced


SIJ provocation cluster
Perform distraction, compression, thigh thrust, sacral thrust, and Gaenslen; >=3 positive is meaningful
Sacroiliac joint as source rather than the disc if >=3 tests reproduce buttock pain


Facet loading
With the patient standing, extend and rotate the lumbar spine
Facet-mediated pain if paraspinal pain is reproduced with extension (unlike flexion, which provokes discs)

title: Discogenic PainClinical Presentation
text:
Red Flags

Cauda equina syndrome:

New urinary retention or overflow incontinence (most reliable sign)
Saddle (perineal) anesthesia
Fecal incontinence or reduced anal sphincter tone
Bilateral or progressive lower-extremity weakness

Infection (spondylodiscitis, epidural abscess):

Fever
Immunosuppression, HIV, or diabetes
IV drug use, indwelling catheter, or recent infection/spinal procedure

Malignancy:

History of cancer (most useful single flag)
Unexplained weight loss
Age >50 years
Pain worse at night or at rest; no improvement after ~4 weeks

Fracture:

Significant trauma (or minor trauma with osteoporosis, chronic steroids, or age >=75)
Long-term corticosteroid use
Older age

title: Back Pain BasicsPhysical Exam
text: The physical exam should screen function, look for structural clues, assess neurologic status, and use special tests when they fit the clinical picture.

title: Back Pain BasicsPhysical Exam
text:
General functional screen: 3S
Use 3S as a quick screen of function.

Sit-to-stand
Observe whether the patient can rise from a chair comfortably and without assistance.


Stance
Observe whether the patient can fully straighten once standing, maintain balance, and show normal spinal alignment.
Also look for symmetry of the shoulders, hips, and knees.


Stride
Observe gait.
Look for:

Normal gait pattern
Normal stride length
Ability to turn safely and efficiently

title: Back Pain BasicsPhysical Exam
text:
Special tests
The following are a few useful special tests for common back pain generators; they are not an exhaustive list. More complete test descriptions and interpretation are provided in the individual modules.
Spinal deformity:

Adam’s forward bend test: Assesses spinal symmetry while the patient bends forward at the hips; asymmetry of the spine or shoulders may suggest scoliosis.
Modified Schober’s test: Measures lumbar flexion and may identify restriction seen in inflammatory conditions such as axial spondyloarthritis.

Radicular pain:

Straight leg raise: Reproduces radiating leg pain when the symptomatic leg is raised while the patient is supine; hamstring tightness alone is not a positive test.
Lasègue sign: Re-tensions the sciatic nerve with ankle dorsiflexion after a positive straight leg raise.
Crossed straight leg raise: Reproduction of symptoms in the affected leg is more specific for disc herniation.




Source: Wikimedia Commons.


Sacroiliac joint pain:

FABER: Stresses the SI joint with the hip in a figure-four position; posterior pelvic or buttock pain supports SI joint involvement, whereas groin pain suggests hip pathology.
Gaenslen’s test: Stresses the SI joint by extending one hip while flexing the other, and may reproduce posterior pelvic or buttock pain.
