title: SpasticityRelevant Anatomy
text: The mechanisms and pathways that underlie the development of spasticity have not been fully elucidated. Presently, the main identifying factors are abnormal intraspinal processing of afferent signals, loss of descending supraspinal inhibition of reflex arcs, decreased inhibitory control of corticospinal tracts, and increased motor neuron excitability. The following sections offer an overview of the relevant anatomy.

title: SpasticityRelevant Anatomy
text:
Big Picture
The cerebral cortex is essential for sending commands for voluntary movement. The frontal motor area forms corticospinal pathways. Premotor and supplementary motor cortices are important for sequencing and modulating voluntary movements. The prefrontal cortex plans movement, while parietal areas guide movement. Association areas use conscious and unconscious information to further guide movement.
Subcortical centers, including the basal ganglia and cerebellum, maintain tone, posture, and coordination. The brainstem, particularly the pons and medullary reticular nuclei, vestibular nuclei, and red nuclei, is an important station that modulates stretch reflexes, posture, and repetitive movements.
The spinal cord contains complex neuronal circuits and is also the area of interface between upper and lower motor neurons. It involves:

Motor unit: A motor neuron and all the muscle fibers it innervates.
Spinal cord reflexes.




Source: PMC.

title: SpasticityRelevant Anatomy
text:
Reflex Pathways
In healthy individuals, stretch reflexes are mediated by excitatory connections between alpha motor neurons and the Ia afferent fibers from muscle spindles. Passive stretch of the muscle excites muscle spindles, causing Ia fibers to fire and send input to alpha motor neurons through spinal pathways. The alpha motor neurons send an efferent impulse to the muscle, causing it to contract.
Golgi tendon organs sense tension and send signals via Ib afferents. Golgi tendon organ Ib afferents provide inhibitory input in response to muscle tension, helping regulate excessive contraction.



Source: David G. Behm, The Science and Physiology of Flexibility and Stretching.


In patients with spasticity, the stretch reflex is exaggerated. Two theoretical causes are:

Increased excitability of muscle spindles.
Abnormal processing of sensory inputs from normal muscle spindles in the spinal cord. This is the more widely accepted theory.

title: SpasticityRelevant Anatomy
text:
Descending Pathways of Control

Corticospinal Tract
The corticospinal tract is important for voluntary motor control and also receives and modulates inputs from other sources. Lesions of the corticospinal tract alone do not usually cause spasticity; involvement of other tracts is generally required.



Source: ResearchGate.




Reticulospinal Tract
The reticulospinal tract is the pathway most commonly implicated in spasticity. The dorsal reticulospinal pathway is inhibitory to the stretch reflex, while the medial, or pontine, reticulospinal tract is facilitatory. Therefore, when only the dorsal tract is disturbed, the system is pushed toward hyperexcitability.
Direct evidence shows upregulated reticulospinal output in subjects who develop spasticity after spinal cord injury.





Vestibulospinal Tract
The vestibulospinal tract facilitates extensor tone and is important in maintaining posture and balance. Its unopposed activity can cause increased tone.



Source: ScienceDirect.

title: SpasticityRelevant Anatomy
text:
Muscle Fibers and Extracellular Matrix
Skeletal muscle is organized hierarchically: whole muscle → fascicle → muscle fiber → myofibril → sarcomere.
The muscle fiber is the basic cellular unit of skeletal muscle. It is multinucleated and bound by the sarcolemma. A myofibril is composed of serially repeating sarcomeres joined at Z-lines. Sarcomeres are the smallest fundamental contractile units. They are formed by myosin and actin filaments, which form cross-bridges and shorten in a process driven by ATP.
In spasticity, fiber-level architecture is disrupted.



Source: Nature.


The extracellular matrix contains three connective tissue layers:

Endomysium: The innermost layer of collagen fibers, which anchors onto the sarcolemma and is important for lateral force transmission.
Perimysium: Surrounds each fascicle and carries blood vessels and nerves. Large collagen fibers are a site of pathological stiffening in contractures.
Epimysium: The outermost dense collagen sheath around the whole muscle. It helps transmit force from fibers to the skeleton.




Source: Gillies AR, Lieber RL. Structure and Function of the Skeletal Muscle Extracellular Matrix.


In spasticity, many changes occur at the extracellular matrix and muscle fiber levels. For example, there may be a reduced number of sarcomeres, or sarcomeres may be held at longer-than-optimal lengths.
Passive fiber mechanics are typically unaltered, and increased stiffness is usually due to alterations in the extracellular matrix. Collagen accumulates in contracted muscle, which directly increases stiffness.

title: SpondylolisthesisAdvanced Topics
text:
Spondylolysis is the most common identifiable cause of adolescent low back pain, with a prevalence of approximately 4–8% that is higher in athletes participating in hyperextension sports. Pediatric slips are usually isthmic, arising from a pars fatigue fracture caused by repetitive loading in a genetically predisposed patient. The rarer dysplastic type, characterized by deficient L5–S1 posterior elements, carries a high risk of high-grade progression.



Slip progression occurs during growth and largely halts at skeletal maturity, so risk peaks around the adolescent growth spurt. Monitor asymptomatic slips radiographically until growth is complete. Dysplastic slips should be followed with radiographs every 6–9 months.



Nonoperative care is first-line and includes activity restriction, flexion-based core therapy, and, when appropriate, bracing. About two-thirds of acute pars lesions unite with early rest.
Reserve surgery, including instrumented fusion and occasionally direct pars repair, for symptoms refractory to at least six months of care, high-grade or progressive slips, or neurologic deficit.






NoteKey idea



Pediatric disease is usually isthmic and growth-driven. The classic pattern is extension-provoked back pain, hamstring tightness, and painful mobility without radiculopathy. Dysplastic slips are the exception and require close surveillance for high-grade progression.

title: SpondylolisthesisAdvanced Topics
text:
High-grade spondylolisthesis

Definition and features
High-grade spondylolisthesis is defined as at least 50% slip, corresponding to Meyerding grades III–V. Grade V, or spondyloptosis, is a slip greater than 100%.
High-grade disease can produce lumbosacral kyphosis and sagittal malalignment. Findings include severe hamstring tightness, trunk shortening, a palpable step-off, and the crouched Phalen-Dickson gait. L5 radiculopathy, and rarely cauda equina syndrome, is more frequent, and nonoperative treatment is less reliable.


Management
Symptomatic high-grade slips are treated surgically. Options include:

In situ posterior instrumented fusion: Commonly extending from L4 to S1 and often reinforced with iliac or transsacral fixation; this remains the long-standing standard.
Reduction: May improve sagittal alignment and lower pseudarthrosis rates without a significant increase in neurologic deficits, but carries a risk of traction injury to the L5 root.
Spondyloptosis procedures: Posterior spinal shortening or partial L5 spondylectomy, such as the Gaines procedure, may be used to correct severe lumbosacral kyphosis.

title: SpondylolisthesisClassification and Etiology
text:
Spondylolysis refers to a defect or elongation of the pars interarticularis, occurring on one or both sides of the vertebral arch and most often at L5. Spondylolisthesis, by contrast, denotes actual displacement of a vertebra relative to the one directly below it, usually in the forward direction.
The two lie on a spectrum linked by the bilateral pars lesion. When both sides of the arch are defective, the posterior bony “hook” that normally restrains forward movement is lost, allowing the vertebra to translate anteriorly and converting isolated spondylolysis into isthmic spondylolisthesis.



Source: OrthoInfo / AAOS.








NoteKey idea



Spondylolysis is a pars defect; spondylolisthesis is actual vertebral slip. A bilateral pars lesion allows lysis to progress to isthmic listhesis, often silently during the adolescent growth spurt.

title: SpondylolisthesisClassification and Etiology
text:
Etiologic classification: Wiltse-Newman
The Wiltse-Newman classification sorts spondylolisthesis by its underlying cause.



Source: Orthobullets.



Dysplastic
Dysplastic, or developmental, slips arise from malformation of the lumbosacral junction, typically with deficient posterior elements at L5–S1. They characteristically occur at L5–S1, are associated with spina bifida occulta, and carry a disproportionately high risk of progressing to high-grade slippage. This tendency may reflect a growth deficiency of the upper sacrum and is strongly linked to elevated pelvic incidence and other abnormal spinopelvic parameters.


Isthmic
Isthmic slips result from a pars interarticularis lesion and are subclassified as lytic, elongated-but-intact pars, or acute pars fracture. The lytic form is most common: a stress fracture from repetitive loading, often occurring in the setting of genetic predisposition. MRI can detect marrow edema before a discrete fracture line appears.
Isthmic disease predominates in the lower lumbar spine and is the form most often seen in young athletes engaged in repetitive hyperextension and rotation.


Degenerative
Degenerative spondylolisthesis develops from age-related deterioration of the intervertebral disc and facet joints, without a pars defect. Progressive disc-height loss and facet incompetence permit the vertebra to slip forward, most commonly at L4–L5.
It is a disease of older adults, is more frequent in women, and is a leading contributor to lumbar spinal stenosis.


Traumatic
Traumatic slips follow acute injury to the posterior bony restraints, typically multiple fractures of the neural arch or, much less commonly, an isolated bilateral fracture of the pars interarticularis. This category is distinct from the fatigue-type pars lesion of isthmic disease because it results from a single high-energy event.


Pathologic
Pathologic spondylolisthesis occurs when bone or joint architecture is weakened by an underlying disease process, most often infection or a benign or malignant tumor that destroys the elements maintaining vertebral alignment. Generalized or localized bone disease can likewise compromise the posterior bony restraint, permitting slippage.


Iatrogenic
Iatrogenic spondylolisthesis develops as a consequence of medical or surgical intervention, such as destabilizing bone or facet structures during decompression or other spinal procedures.

title: SpondylolisthesisDiagnosis
text:
Isthmic disease commonly presents with activity-related axial pain worsened by extension, rotation, and loading. Degenerative disease presents in older adults and often includes neurogenic claudication.
Key findings include segmental tenderness, painful or limited extension, hamstring tightness, and a focused neurologic examination assessing strength, sensation, reflexes, and straight-leg raise. These findings are more sensitive than specific, and pain-free extension does not exclude the diagnosis.

title: SpondylolisthesisDiagnosis
text:
Plain radiographs
Standing lateral radiographs are the initial test for detecting and grading a slip. Upright positioning is essential because a slip may reduce when the patient is supine. Anteroposterior and lateral views can demonstrate both spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis.



“A sagittal radiograph depicting grade II spondylolisthesis located between the L4-L5.” Source: Radiopaedia.

title: SpondylolisthesisDiagnosis
text:
Flexion-extension radiographs
Standing flexion-extension views are the traditional standard for detecting dynamic instability, which can influence surgical planning. However, their reliability is debated because they may underestimate instability. Upright radiographs combined with supine MRI, or natural sitting lateral views, may detect unstable cases more effectively.

title: SpondylolisthesisDiagnosis
text:
Computed tomography
CT provides the best bony detail for characterizing a pars defect, including cortical integrity, fracture acuity, and sclerosis. It is also useful for surgical planning. CT or CT myelography can assess neural compression when MRI is contraindicated. Radiation exposure is an important consideration in young patients.

title: SpondylolisthesisDiagnosis
text:
Magnetic resonance imaging
MRI is the best noninvasive test for evaluating neural compression in the central canal, lateral recesses, and neural foramina, and it avoids radiation. In adolescents, MRI can detect an early stress reaction with marrow edema before a frank fracture develops.
A facet effusion greater than 1.5 mm on supine MRI suggests a reducible degenerative slip and should prompt standing radiographs.

Assessment of spinal and spinopelvic alignment
Full-length standing radiographs allow measurement of spinopelvic parameters that guide progression risk assessment and surgical planning. Important measurements include pelvic incidence, pelvic tilt, sacral slope, lumbar lordosis, and sagittal vertical axis.
Pelvic incidence is fixed and individual-specific:

High pelvic incidence is associated with both isthmic and degenerative disease and correlates with slip grade and progression.

title: SpondylolisthesisManagement
text:
Most symptomatic spondylolysis and low-grade spondylolisthesis respond to nonoperative care. This is the appropriate first-line approach for patients without a neurologic deficit.
Core components include:

Activity modification and load management: Temporarily stop aggravating, especially extension-based, sports. Athletes typically rest for approximately six weeks, then gradually return based on symptoms.
Physical therapy: Emphasize core and trunk stabilization, hamstring flexibility, and correction of postural and biomechanical factors. Physical therapy is the most consistently appropriate nonoperative measure across clinical scenarios.
NSAIDs: Use for pain control when clinically appropriate.
Epidural or transforaminal steroid injections: Consider when radicular symptoms are prominent.
Bracing: A TLSO may be used chiefly in pediatric or adolescent cases. Its value is debated because healing and return-to-play outcomes may be similar with or without bracing.







NoteKey idea



In pediatric patients, dysplastic spondylolisthesis carries a higher risk of progression and warrants surveillance radiographs every 6–9 months.

title: SpondylolisthesisManagement
text:
Indications for surgery
Surgery is considered for patients who fail at least six months of conservative management or who have higher-risk features. Key indications include:

High-grade slip, defined as Meyerding grade III–V
Progression of slippage, such as progression by more than one grade or documented instability
Neurologic deficit, persistent or refractory radiculopathy, or neurogenic claudication
Documented instability, including at least 5 mm of translation or at least 20° greater angular motion than the adjacent level on flexion-extension imaging in isthmic disease

title: SpondylolisthesisManagement
text:
Surgical management
Surgical strategy is tailored to slip type, grade, and the presence of stenosis or instability.

Decompression with or without fusion
In degenerative spondylolisthesis, decompression alone has been shown to be noninferior to decompression plus fusion in selected patients. Fusion may reduce recurrent slip but adds morbidity and cost, so it is reserved mainly for dynamically unstable segments or situations in which decompression would create instability.


Fusion techniques
Posterolateral fusion, with or without pedicle screws, and interbody techniques such as TLIF, PLIF, ALIF, and OLIF are options. For low-grade isthmic disease, these techniques produce similar outcomes in many patients; circumferential fusion adds risk without clear benefit in routine cases.


Reduction versus in situ fusion
Reduction improves deformity correction and may lower pseudarthrosis rates but offers no clear pain or functional benefit in low-grade slips. Its main role is in selected high-grade cases, where alignment and lumbosacral kyphosis are major concerns.


Pars repair
Direct pars repair is a motion-preserving option in young patients with isolated spondylolysis or a very low-grade slip, particularly when the disc and facet joints remain healthy.
